To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the cloud microphysics and turbulent structure observed at UFS were representative of those in other clouds, with a few notable differences in the microphysical properties, and the cloud turbulence was consistent with the high-Reynolds number turbulence observed in other flows, including the atmosphere.

the observed turbulence is consistent with the Kolmogoroff–Kraichnan theory for high-Reynold’s number flows, the observed clouds have size distributions typical of warm clouds and are characterized by liquid water contents of 1 g/m3, and the observed fluctuations in liquid water content and droplet number concentration are consistent with inhomogeneous mixing.

turbulence and cloud microphysics are coupled in a warm continental cloud, with microphysical processes influencing turbulence through the phase relaxation time and turbulence influencing microphysical processes through inhomogeneous mixing.

the study of the microphysical and turbulent structure of warm clouds, and the interactions between these two components, using high-resolution in situ measurements.
the interaction between turbulence and cloud microphysics, and the results presented here are a first step toward understanding the nature of the interactions.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the cloud microphysics and the turbulence are not coupled in any way, but rather the turbulence is simply the background against which the microphysics is observed.

the observed cloud–turbulent interactions are consistent with the expectations of the theory of homogeneous isotropic turbulence, with the exception of the enhanced high-frequency variance of the liquid water content, which suggests that the cloud microphysics are not completely decoupled from the turbulence.

the clouds observed at UFS are representative of typical continental clouds, and the measurements presented here are representative of the state of the art of in situ measurements of cloud–turbulance interactions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the turbulence observed in these clouds is consistent with the turbulence of the free atmosphere.
the turbulence observed in these warm clouds is consistent with the high-Reynolds number scaling, and that the microphysics is consistent with a turbulent cloud environment.
we can expect the same physics to govern the interaction between clouds and turbulence in the Alps as in the tropics.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the UFS station is a suitable location for high-resolution measurements of cloud microphysics, turbulence, and their interaction.
the microphysics and turbulence of clouds are not only well represented at the mountain station, but the data are also suitable for detailed studies of turbulence–microphysics interactions.
mountain top stations are suitable for high-resolution cloud–turbulance measurements and can be used to complement airborne measurements.
